first_pass.notes: Core model and the cooperator/defector domain dynamics are textbook. The documented noise is C->D or symmetric, while this rule is D->C (mirror image). I found no paper that studies the one-way D->C case directly, but it is a small, expected perturbation. The non-textbook fingerprint (nearly all-C world with defector islands, declining activity) is probably a consequence of the D->C source. I did not read full texts of the Nowak/Mukherji papers and did not search for the S=-0.5 two-game variants.

full_text:
**Verdict: KNOWN.** This is the Nowak–May spatial Prisoner's Dilemma with a small amount of strategy-mutation noise. Nothing in what was observed needs a new explanation, and the "domain coarsening" signal is most likely the system running down into a near-absorbing, cooperator-dominated state rather than real emergent coarsening.

**Why it's known**
- **The core model is textbook.** Payoffs R=1, P=0, S=0, T=b with b between 1 and 2, on a lattice with deterministic copy-the-best-neighbour updating, is the Nowak–May parameterization of the spatial PD. The original authors studied PD on a two dimensional array with synchronous updating and explored the asymptotic behavior for various values of the parameter b.
- **Noise toward cooperation is already covered.** Mukherji et al. tested perturbations including random introduction of cooperators and defectors at any site and spontaneous conversion of cooperators into defectors with some probability. Nowak et al. replied stating that, their results are robust with respect to these modifications. The one-way defector-to-cooperator flip here is just the cooperator half of "random introduction of cooperators and defectors".
- **The exact payoff and this noise direction appear in Helbing & Yu.** Their imitation-plus-noise runs use T=1.3, R=1, P=0.1, S=0, and their figures mark each defector who became a cooperator as a separate category. Their P=0.1 differs slightly from P=0 here. I did not find a paper on purely one-way D→C noise, but by the stated criterion an undocumented rule combination is not a discovery.

**Why the fingerprint isn't textbook (my reasoning, not checked against a source)**
- b=1.3 is in the low-temptation range of Nowak–May. There, cooperators dominate and defectors survive only as small static or oscillating clusters. You don't get the 1.8<b<2 "spatial chaos" regime with its kaleidoscope patterns and roughly 0.318 cooperator fraction.
- Because the noise only ever turns defectors into cooperators, all-cooperator is an absorbing state. The noise wears away the leftover defector clusters, and nothing creates new defectors.
- That fits every observed feature:
  - largest domain ≈0.935, meaning the cooperator sea;
  - a few remaining domains;
  - activity falling over time;
  - a single reversal.
- So passing the "coarsening" and "spatial game chaos" tests is a side effect of the metrics. This is relaxation toward a frozen or absorbing state, not curvature-driven coarsening and not sustained chaos.

**Caveat on the class grouping.** The other programs listed in the same class use different noise (a COPY rule) and a second game (1.5, −0.5). Their behaviour should match only if they also end up in a cooperator-dominated, nearly frozen state. I did not verify that.
